**Search is only as useful as the signal deciding where to search.** MCTS repeatedly chooses branches, evaluates them, and uses those evaluations to allocate more trials. A process reward model scores intermediate reasoning steps. This seems attractive because an early correct step can receive credit before the final answer is known. The difficulty is that “looks like a good step” and “actually preserves a valid solution” can differ. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050)

Imagine a scorer that favors polished algebra and familiar phrases. Search can discover a branch that repeats convincing-looking manipulations while making one subtle invalid cancellation. Once that branch receives a high score, search spends more compute extending the mistake. Optimizing against a learned evaluator exposes weaknesses that ordinary held-out prediction tests may miss.

**The target also moves.** As the policy changes, it generates new styles and mistakes. The value model must remain accurate on those new trajectories, including partial solutions unlike its training examples. Reliable step labels can be expensive or ambiguous: an unusual but valid route might look worse than a conventional dead end.

A rule-based final verifier can provide a simpler target: the submitted program passes tests, or the mathematical answer matches a trusted check. Group-relative optimization can then compare sampled outcomes without a separate learned critic. That trades away dense guidance and does not eliminate incomplete tests or reward hacking. MCTS and PRMs remain useful when intermediate states can be verified reliably; the comparison is about verifier quality and cost, not a universal failure of search.

**Technical details and references.**

Tree search amplifies whatever its value/process scorer favors. If a scorer rewards plausible-looking but incorrect steps, search discovers those weaknesses; changing policies also shift the distribution on which the value model must be accurate. Fine-grained labeling and long branching searches add substantial cost. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)

Verifiable outcome rewards avoid some learned-judge ambiguity, and group-relative baselines remove a separately trained critic. They still suffer sparse rewards, test incompleteness, and reward hacking. This is not proof that MCTS/PRMs universally fail: they can help when intermediate verification and search structure are strong. Compare correctness at equal total compute and audit the verifier itself. A broken test suite gives a precisely optimized but wrong target regardless of the RL algorithm.
